item.title: 66% of billion-dollar companies leave critical bugs unpatched — the part the AI bug-hunting hype leaves out
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:

The post 66% of billion-dollar companies leave critical bugs unpatched — the part the AI bug-hunting hype leaves out appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Chainguard has launched an AI-powered security harness that uses frontier models, including Anthropic’s restricted Claude Mythos 5.1, to find and fix exploitable vulnerabilities in application code that conventional scanners miss.

Developers can use Chainguard Harness without direct access to Mythos, but the company hasn’t disclosed which models handle vulnerability discovery for those customers.

The company says Harness has found serious vulnerabilities in codebases that had already undergone extensive security scanning, including software used in critical infrastructure. Details about the affected projects, the flaws themselves, and their remediation status remain undisclosed.

Announced Wednesday, Harness leads a four-product launch alongside Workspaces, Checks, and expanded Libraries protections, extending Chainguard’s reach beyond hardened container images and dependencies into agent execution environments and CI verification.

Mythos access without Glasswing

Anthropic has restricted Claude Mythos 5.1 access to organizations participating in Project Glasswing, leaving open which models Harness customers outside the program will use.

Harness will also be available through Anthropic’s Claude Marketplace, allowing teams to use existing Anthropic spending commitments rather than secure a separate budget.

The AI exploit gap

The launches come alongside The AI Exploit Gap, a Chainguard-commissioned Wakefield Research survey of 1,300 security leaders across nine markets. More than half said their organizations knowingly leave high or critical vulnerabilities unpatched at least sometimes, with the figure reaching 66% at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue, compared with 27% at companies below $250 million.

“AI can find and chain flaws in minutes, while fixing them still moves at human speed and competes with product deadlines and uptime,” Quincy Castro, Chainguard’s chief information security officer, said in a statement. “Patching faster isn’t viable for most folks, and it will consume increasing amounts of resources just to keep pace.”

“AI can find and chain flaws in minutes, while fixing them still moves at human speed and competes with product deadlines and uptime”

Isolated microVMs for agents

Each developer and coding agent gets a hardware-isolated microVM with network policies that restrict access to internal systems.

Credentials stay outside the agent’s environment, limiting what a compromised agent or malicious dependency can reach. Signed activity logs record what each agent did so teams can keep an audit trail across multiple autonomous sessions.

CI inside the agent loop

Chainguard Checks lets coding agents run CI checks directly during development and receive signed results in seconds. Agents can run tests, inspect failures, and revise code before opening a pull request, avoiding the CI queues that become harder to manage as vendors like Cognition, Microsoft, and Augment Code turn coding agents into shared team infrastructure running multiple sessions in parallel.

To avoid rebuilding environments on every run, Checks uses warm snapshots with dependencies already installed and refreshes them in the background when the lockfile changes. Each workflow step runs in a separate hardware-isolated microVM built from Chainguard OS packages, including FIPS-compliant toolchains. With Workspaces, agent sessions pause during verification and resume with structured failure logs in context.

With Workspaces, agent sessions pause during verification and resume with structured failure logs in context.

Runners never hold long-lived credentials. Instead, a host-side proxy injects short-lived credentials into outbound requests, while declarative egress policies restrict network access and can terminate a microVM if it attempts an unauthorized connection. Successful runs produce signed attestations tied to the execution environment, test results, and commit, which merge gates can verify without rerunning the suite. Checks is available now in beta.

Libraries Lock Down Late-Breaking Bugs

Chainguard Libraries is adding secure package endpoints for Go and .NET, along with CVE remediation for JavaScript, and Go. Java and Python support will also expand to cover newly disclosed vulnerabilities discovered through AI-assisted research, including flaws in dependencies that coding agents may have already pulled into a project.

Chainguard Libraries is adding secure package endpoints for Go and .NET, along with CVE remediation for JavaScript, and Go.

The changes build on Chainguard Repository, a policy-enforced endpoint for open source dependencies, and its partnership with Cursor, allowing coding agents to resolve packages through Chainguard’s catalog instead of pulling directly from public registries.

Chainguard’s new Harness points frontier models like Claude Mythos 5.1 at your code, alongside new tools to isolate coding agents and verify their work.

item.title: Anthropic’s red team ran AI on 15 cheap TV boxes. Then the math got unsettling.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
For roughly $825, Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team built a cluster of 15 off-brand Android TV boxes that runs an AI

The post Anthropic’s red team ran AI on 15 cheap TV boxes. Then the math got unsettling. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
For roughly $825, Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team built a cluster of 15 off-brand Android TV boxes that runs an AI model at 0.39 tokens per second, painfully slow for a chatbot but fine for software with nowhere to be and nobody waiting on it.

That experiment anchors new research from Anthropic researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, published Monday, suggesting small open-weight models may be only months away from copying themselves across cheap, internet-connected hardware without relying on a datacenter.

The researchers haven’t built an AI worm that can spread across the public internet on its own, and their experiments took place inside controlled environments with shortcuts that made replication easier. But the results suggest several of the remaining technical barriers may be temporary.

The researchers haven’t built an AI worm that can spread across the public internet on its own, and their experiments took place inside controlled environments with shortcuts that made replication easier.

Inference is the real hurdle

Zhou and Freeman identify four steps an AI needs to take to replicate itself, which are finding a target, gaining access, getting inference running, and moving on to the next machine.

Previous benchmarks such as CyberGym and ExploitBench suggest smaller models can already handle some of the exploitation work, and frontier agents escaped their test sandboxes using basic exploits earlier this year. The bigger challenge may be getting a model running on unfamiliar hardware, where it has to sort out whatever operating system, dependencies, and installation problems it runs into.

In Anthropic’s tests, Qwen3.5-9B deployed a working Llama3.1-8B inference server on eight of nine hardware types, including Jetson Nanos, Macs, and RTX 4090 machines, while the larger GLM-5.2 handled the same work more reliably and with higher throughput.

The team then built a firewalled Google Cloud environment with eight nodes running Android emulators, and starting from a single worm instance, the system had to reach the other nodes and establish a working inference server on each one. A fresh copy of the worm was spawned whenever a node’s server passed correctness and anti-cheating checks, and GLM-5.2 reached all eight nodes in four of five trials and seven nodes in the fifth.

GLM-5.2 ran on a separate inference server because the target machines couldn’t hold it, so the worm installed a smaller 8B model in its place, and the researchers made exploitation easy by leaving an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge port open.

A fresh copy of the worm was spawned whenever a node’s server passed correctness and anti-cheating checks, and GLM-5.2 reached all eight nodes in four of five trials and seven nodes in the fifth.

Worms that take notes

The agents got better at setting up inference on unfamiliar hardware when they could read notes left by earlier attempts. The researchers ran Qwen3.5-9B through 20 separate lineages, each lasting six generations, and success climbed from 45% in the first generation to between 61% and 84% in later ones.

The researchers call this Lamarckian inheritance, where one agent passes what it learned to the next without any retraining of the model. It’s a mechanism familiar to developers using persistent agent runtimes such as OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, but here that memory helps successive copies work through installation failures on hardware they’ve never seen.

The researchers call this Lamarckian inheritance, where one agent passes what it learned to the next without any retraining of the model

The team also tried giving Qwen3.5-9B access to the much more capable Opus 4.8 model for advice, and it produced no statistically significant improvement because the small model tended not to know the right questions to ask.

The end-of-2026 trend line

The paper identifies two constraints that have kept this scenario theoretical. A model needs to be capable enough to replicate reliably and small enough to run on compromised hardware, and right now those requirements don’t overlap. GLM-5.2 showed the necessary competence in the simplified test but is too large for the cheap devices the researchers have in mind, while smaller models can fit on those devices, particularly when inference is distributed across several machines, but can’t yet complete the entire process consistently.

Using the Epoch Capabilities Index, the researchers tracked open-weight models with 30 billion parameters or fewer and found that, by the end of 2026, the trend line puts the strongest of them at GLM-5.2’s general capability level. It’s a rough estimate, since general capability scores don’t necessarily predict replication performance, and the team’s end-to-end experiment used favorable conditions.

By the researchers’ calculations, typical 4GB TV boxes running 4-bit weights can host a 9B model across four or more devices, and a 26B model across ten or more, which is how their own 15-box cluster runs Gemma4-26B-A4B.

A single inference setup on this class of hardware could take roughly 28 to 150 hours depending on the model, and the researchers argue that lightweight agents may be far more willing than human attackers to grind through that kind of effort across huge numbers of devices. They compare the possibility to a digital slime mold, spreading slowly through whatever resources it can reach.

Cheap boxes, borrowed compute

The Kimwolf botnet infected more than two million devices, most of them cheap Android TV boxes, and the researchers used that figure to calculate what an AI replicator could do with a network of equivalent size. Dividing those devices into clusters of 15 running Gemma4-26B-A4B would yield roughly 133,000 copies of the model generating a combined 80,000 tokens per second.

That’s equivalent to no more than about 40 Nvidia H100 GPUs, which is modest by datacenter standards, but the hardware and operating costs would belong to someone else.

The researchers also examined edge accelerators such as Nvidia Jetsons, which are used in everything from security cameras and conference room equipment to robots and drones. Those devices are generally harder to reach because they communicate through outbound cloud-management connections.

Stopping software that copies itself

The researchers aren’t suggesting there’s no way to stop a self-replicating AI worm, and some of its traits could make it easier to detect. Moving multi-gigabyte models between devices creates network traffic that ISPs can monitor, and a worm that spreads aggressively won’t go unnoticed.

During the Mirai botnet cleanup, one ISP’s quarantine of infected subscribers cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, and the researchers expect a similar approach to work as a first line of defense. Eliminating a replicator completely, however, would mean coordinating every ISP with infected customers.

Anthropic ran an AI model on 15 cheap Android TV boxes, and its research suggests small open-weight models could soon self-replicate across IoT devices.

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon debuts with a unified 1M input/output token limit
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
On Tuesday, Google made Gemini 4 Argon, the company’s new flagship model, available to developers on the paid tier of

The post Gemini 4 Argon debuts with a unified 1M input/output token limit appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, Google made Gemini 4 Argon, the company’s new flagship model, available to developers on the paid tier of the Gemini API through Google AI Studio, as well as in several of the company’s other developer and consumer tools.

Google announced the model on September 30. Initial external access was limited to selected cyber defenders in its Fairwind Program and other trusted testers; Google employees were also using it internally.

Gemini 4 Argon pricing

Google is giving the model a competitive price. Developers will pay an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, with a single 1 million-token budget for input and output combined. That’s the same price as OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol.

After that date, Google’s new model will cost $4 and $20 per million tokens, matching Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5. Cached input tokens are 95 percent off during the introductory period.

During the introductory period, Argon also costs a fifth of what Anthropic charges for Claude Fable 5.1 and OpenAI charges for GPT-6 Astra, which both list at $10 and $50 per million tokens.

Developers can call the model as gemini-4-argon through Google’s Interactions API, with support in the google-genai SDKs. Android developers can also build it into their apps through Firebase AI Logic.

One budget for input and output

Argon’s unified 1 million input/output token limit covers both what goes into the model and what comes out of it, according to Google. That’s markedly different from how Google described it in the original Sept. 30 Argon announcement. At the time, it called the limit an output cap of 1 million tokens, up from 64,000 in earlier Gemini models.

With what is now a shared budget, the equation changes a bit because a long prompt can now eat into how much the model can write back. For example, if a request loads 800,000 tokens of code, that leaves only 200,000 for the response.

In comparison, Claude Opus 5.5 combines the standard 1 million-token context window with a separate output cap of 128,000 tokens.

Google says the extra room will let Argon keep working on long, multistep coding, science, and agent jobs.

Gemini 4 Argon benchmarks

Google says Argon ranks first on the Vals Index, which scores models on finance, coding, legal, and tax work and weights each sector by its share of U.S. GDP.

On Embodied Reasoning Question Answering (ERQA), a test of physical and spatial reasoning, Google reports Argon scored 87 percent. That puts it ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 at 82.3 percent, GPT-6 Astra at 81 percent, and Claude Fable 5.1 at 74 percent.

Bloomberg reported Sept. 30 that some Google employees with access to the model said it struggled with certain coding tasks, particularly front-end design. Google told Bloomberg it would be “inaccurate to say that Gemini 4 is underperforming in areas such as coding.”

For now, we don’t have a full set of new benchmarks to better compare Argon to other models. Like some other frontier labs, Google focused its announcement more on “feels” than data. Benchmarks never tell the full story, but we’ll update this post once we hear more. Artificial Analysis published an evaluation on September 30: Argon scored 53 on its Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra at the models’ tested reasoning settings. However, there’s no guarantee the model released on Tuesday is precisely the same as the one tested on September 30.

Argon in Antigravity

Where else Argon is available is a bit complicated.

For coding, Google is also making Argon available in Antigravity, its platform for running coding agents across the editor, terminal, and browser. Argon is available in the Antigravity desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux and in the Antigravity CLI, but only for Google AI Ultra subscribers and eligible Gemini Enterprise plans.

AI Pro subscribers get Argon in the Gemini app, but not in Antigravity.

Google is also bringing Antigravity’s coding interface into the Gemini app for macOS, so users can move between chatting and coding without switching tools. Anthropic and OpenAI do the same with their Claude and ChatGPT/Codex desktop apps, but nobody has found an elegant way to combine these chat and coding tools into a single interface.

In Android Studio Canary, developers can sign in to Antigravity from the agent tool window, and a new Android CLI plugin gives the agent access to local Android build tools.

More than 100,000 Googlers use Argon each month in an in-house build of Antigravity, the company says. Over four weeks, code submitted by agents rose 35 percent while post-submit rollbacks fell 30 percent.

Google says more than half of its Cloud sales staff and almost half of its finance team now use Antigravity.

Argon in the Gemini app

Subscribers on Google’s AI Pro and Ultra plans now also get access to Argon in the Gemini app and in AI Mode in Search.

In addition to the new model, the Gemini app is also getting a new toggle that lets users turn a chat into a task, which Gemini can then keep working on after the user steps away from the computer.

Cyber defenders and agent safety

Google is also expanding Fairwind, the program it launched September 2 to give vetted security teams early access to its cyber models.

Selected Fairwind partners can access Argon without its cyber guardrails, and Google says it’s adding hundreds more partners to the more than 650 the program had when it launched.

For the public model now available, Google says it trained Argon to check with a person before doing anything it can’t undo and to report when it hits a wall instead of working around it.

On coding evaluations, Argon tried unauthorized shortcuts 2 percent of the time, the company says, its lowest rate for any Gemini model (though 2 percent still isn’t zero, and when thousands of agents work together, 2 percent is still quite a few agents that could go rogue).

Google also runs a separate monitor that reads the agent’s reasoning and actions as it works and blocks unintended workarounds. The company says it ran that monitor during training without penalizing the model for what it was thinking, so its reasoning stays readable.

According to Google, Argon also leads Gray Swan’s indirect prompt injection benchmark, with attacks succeeding 0.7 percent of the time across 15 adaptive attempts.

Developers have until November 30 to test Argon at the introductory rate. After that, Argon and Opus 5.5 cost the same per token.

The post Gemini 4 Argon debuts with a unified 1M input/output token limit appeared first on The New Stack.
Two weeks after a cyber-defenders-only debut, Google’s new flagship hits the Gemini API at $2/$10 per million input/output tokens.

item.title: The agent did the work. The audit log couldn’t say who asked.
item.dc:creator: TNS Staff

The post The agent did the work. The audit log couldn’t say who asked. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
More than 20 percent of the MCP-related access policies that Shawn Petty’s team reviewed across customer and prospect environments were broken or missing, according to a recent account published in The New Stack. In most cases, the MCP server ran on someone’s personal token rather than a service account.

At 12 p.m. Eastern/9 a.m. Pacific on Tuesday, October 27, Petty, Chief Customer Officer at CloudBolt, and Mike Bombard, Director of Global Pre-Sales Engineering at CloudBolt, will join The New Stack host Viktor Farcic for a live demo of how to trace an agent’s actions back to the person responsible for them.

The problem, though, usually shows up after an incident: That personal token puts an engineer’s name into the audit trail for everything the agent did. Meanwhile, a shared service account puts the account’s name there instead. In both cases, the audit trail isn’t able to identify who precisely asked the agent to do the work or who approved the access it used.

Access that goes through a request, approval, and grant in the identity provider is provisioned, and the identity provider records it. Access that an agent picks up along the way is emergent: A role inherited from the service that launched it, or a developer’s own token lent out to finish a task. The identity provider holds no record of those grants, so when an agent touches something it shouldn’t, you can’t trace it back.

In this live conversation, the CloudBolt team will explain how agents end up with access nobody approved, then show how to trace that access back to a person with CloudBolt: linking agent activity to your existing identity provider, setting limits on what an agent can touch, and reading the audit trail that results.

Live attendees can ask these experts questions in real time. Register today to join us!

You’ll learn:

  • How to tie agent activity back to your existing identity provider instead of building a parallel system
  • Which infrastructure actions an agent should be allowed to take without a human signing off
  • What a usable audit trail for agent behavior contains, and how to keep one without slowing teams down
  • A live trace of one agent’s credentials and actions, from the task it ran to the person responsible

item.title: Workday is using TypeSafe’s Jev to build user interfaces on the fly
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Workday on Tuesday made Sana, its AI assistant, the new home screen for its HR, finance, and IT software. If

The post Workday is using TypeSafe’s Jev to build user interfaces on the fly appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Workday on Tuesday made Sana, its AI assistant, the new home screen for its HR, finance, and IT software. If you’re not an HR pro, that may not be all that exciting for you, but the way the team built this is maybe one of the most interesting use cases of Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model. Workday is building the user interface on the fly — and all of that is managed by Jev.

In a demo during a press briefing ahead of the announcement, a question about a paycheck brought up a card with the amount hidden behind a click, for example, while a request for time off produced a date picker, with Sana filling in the rest of the form.

Sana, which Workday bought for $1.1 billion last year, is available now, and admins can roll it out to their users without making it the default.

Picking components instead of writing them

Joel Hellermark, Workday’s chief AI officer and Sana’s founder, said in a press briefing that the usual approach to generative UI, in which a model generates the full interface, is “quite slow.”

“If you use a classification model instead and you just give it all of the design components to pick from, you can literally do it instantly,” he said.

Workday gave Jev every atomic component in its design system and hard-coded none of the selection logic, Hellermark said, though the team also had to get data preloading right. In the demo, the paycheck card appeared before he finished typing, for example.

TypeSafe claims Jev answers in 70 to 500 milliseconds, which makes it ideal for this kind of real-time use case.

In many cases, Hellermark said, AI that works through real interface elements does significantly better than pure back-and-forth chat.

A model built to choose

According to TypeSafe, developers send Jev application data and a set of typed questions, and it returns a pick from a list of up to 255 options, a score, or a yes-or-no answer, each with a probability attached. It doesn’t generate text.

TypeSafe launched Jev on Sept. 15 with a $40 million seed round led by DCVC. On Friday, it said it raised an $870 million Series A, led by Andreessen Horowitz, at a $7.5 billion valuation. TypeSafe says a third of the Fortune 500 already use Jev but hasn’t named them. Andreessen Horowitz’s own announcement puts the figure at 25 percent, and TypeSafe’s only published case study features Jack & Jill, an AI recruiting marketplace.

There is no dearth of competition in this field, of course. OpenAI, Amazon, Cloudflare, and Perplexity have already shipped their decision models too, with Microsoft following on last week.

A pattern developers are already testing

Using Jev and similar models for building user interfaces isn’t completely new, though. CopilotKit, an open source framework for adding AI copilots to apps, published a recipe in which Jev picks which prebuilt panel to show, with an OpenAI model as the fallback.

Vercel Labs is testing a Jev mode in json-render, its framework for rendering AI-generated UIs from developer-defined components.

Andrew King, who leads solutions architecture at app developer Very Good Ventures, wrote last month that handing every closed question (one with a fixed set of answers) to Jev cut his generative dashboard’s median render time to 3.8 seconds, from 29 seconds with a frontier model composing it. His tests ran on synthetic data.

“A shape nobody anticipated cannot appear on screen,” King writes. Anything Jev answers with less than 50 percent confidence goes to a language model instead, a setup he calls “a cage with a door.”

In a test on OpenRouter’s blog using the Banking77 intent-classification set, Jev answered in a median 175 milliseconds and scored 81 percent accuracy. Claude Opus 5 scored 84.4 percent but took 2.3 seconds and cost about 22 times as much.

TypeSafe’s own documentation says Jev struggles with counting, arithmetic, and dates, leans toward whichever option is listed first, and doesn’t treat injected content as hostile by default.

Workday hasn’t said how large its design system is or what Sana does when no combination of components fits. King wrote in September that he was keeping client data off Jev because the vendor was “weeks old with no published security certification yet.” TypeSafe now offers a SOC 2 Type II report on request.

What leaves Workday

Workday recently added TypeSafe to its list of subprocessors, the outside companies that can process customer data (the ones you only think about when a SaaS service you subscribe to emails you about a change of subprocessors that you promptly forget). This entry, it’s worth noting, covers all of Workday’s product lines, not just Sana, for natural language processing, intent classification, and confidence scoring.

According to TypeSafe, Jev runs only on its hosted API and processes data in the U.S., and the company offers zero data retention to enterprise customers.

Staying inside Workday

Hellermark also showed Sana working inside Anthropic’s Claude. That’s an AI-to-AI integration, Gerrit Kazmaier, Workday’s president of product and technology, said in the briefing, and users lose the Jev-driven interface and some context along the way.

Workday’s May partnership with Google Cloud already covers A2UI, Google’s spec for agents to describe interfaces that host apps then render. MCP Apps, a Model Context Protocol extension, brings interactive UI into Claude and ChatGPT. Neither shows up in Workday’s announcements this week, so for now, it seems, employees who reach Sana through Claude get the conversation without the date picker.

The post Workday is using TypeSafe’s Jev to build user interfaces on the fly appeared first on The New Stack.
Workday’s AI assistant Sana now builds each screen as you type. Rather than have an LLM draw the interface, TypeSafe’s Jev picks from parts Workday already designed.

item.title: Workday goes headless, opening its HR and finance data to outside AI agents
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Workday is opening up its platform and allowing developers to build their own HR and finance agents in Claude Code,

The post Workday goes headless, opening its HR and finance data to outside AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Workday is opening up its platform and allowing developers to build their own HR and finance agents in Claude Code, Cursor, and other tools, as long as those agents follow the same rules as the people using them.

On Tuesday, at its Workday Rising conference in Las Vegas, the company made its Trusted Agent Platform “headless.”

With this, its Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, SQL access to live Workday data, and a shared runtime for agents are now generally available, and customers can run their own agents on models from Anthropic, Google, Meta, Mistral, Nvidia, and OpenAI.

As Workday CTO Gabe Monroy noted in a press briefing ahead of the event, “No matter who builds the agent, it runs under Workday permissions, approvals and audit trail — no agent gets a side door.”

Workday notes that many companies currently connect their agents to HR and finance data through copies in a data lake or through service accounts, but, the company argues, those approaches bypass those access controls (though companies like SAP, Microsoft, and others would surely argue that they, too, have access control in place).

MCP tools, SQL, and a shared runtime

For AI developers, the main entry point to the Workday ecosystem is Agent-Ready Tools. That’s the company’s MCP server, which ships as part of Workday Extend AI. Users sign in with their own Workday credentials, and Workday says an agent acting for them can’t reach anything their own account can’t. That’s a key feature here, that ties an agent directly to a user’s account.

Monroy said the server currently offers 275 read tools and 54 tools that write or delete data.

Live Data Query, part of Workday Data Cloud, lets BI tools and agents run SQL queries directly against Workday’s data. Monroy described it as JDBC access to Workday’s object graph, and the company says each query returns only what the requesting user is cleared to see.

Three more components are generally available today. Agent Harness is the shared runtime that Workday’s own agents and those built by customers and partners run on. It passes each agent the user’s identity, org position, and access rights, limits what the agent can do, and picks which model handles each task based on cost and performance. Developer Agent generates Workday agents and apps from a natural-language prompt in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or the Workday Developer Site. Custom Agents lets teams deploy agents they built with LangChain or Google’s Agent Development Kit (ADK) onto Agent Harness, though ADK support is limited to design partners for now.

Two more pieces are on the roadmap for early access in early 2027. Agent Context Service will preload only the Workday data a task calls for, which Workday says speeds agents up and limits their exposure to sensitive records. Grounded Reasoning will check a planned action against the customer’s policies, process rules, and Workday records before the agent carries it out.

Workday says customers have built more than 500 agents and more than 6,000 apps with Developer Agent and Agent-Ready Tools in the past four months.

“Headless, the lawless way”

In the briefing, Monroy demoed what he called “headless, the lawless way.” An agent connected to a custom MCP server — a setup he said Workday commonly sees among its customers today — returned job requisitions its user had no business seeing and then moved the wrong employee between teams with no approval. When pointed at a copy of Workday data in Snowflake, the same agent produced the CTO’s salary when asked.

“When it fails, it isn’t just a wrong answer,” Monroy said, “it’s a wrong action that nobody approved.”

When the agent went through Workday’s own MCP server and Data Cloud instead, with the user signed in, the same queries unsurprisingly returned only the requisitions that user was allowed to see (it wouldn’t have been much of a demo of those access controls otherwise, of course).

“A small set of use cases”

Asked whether headless matters as much to Workday as it does to Salesforce, Gerrit Kazmaier, Workday’s president of product and technology, said that Workday is giving customers a choice: “I’d always prefer if they use our user interface, but headless will be equally good.”

Kazmaier noted that building agents directly on Workday’s tools and APIs is “only possible for a small set of use cases where you don’t need to have HR or finance domain logic.” For everything else, he pointed to an AI-to-AI integration in which Claude hands requests to Sana, Workday’s agent orchestrator, which then calls Workday’s own domain agents.

Lakes for analytics, not for agents

It’s worth noting that the Snowflake example is a bit of an awkward one for Workday. When the company announced Data Cloud in September 2025, the pitch included zero-copy sharing of Workday data with Databricks, Salesforce, and Snowflake. Snowflake made its Workday Data Cloud integration generally available on Oct. 7, and Databricks put its Workday connector for Unity Catalog into public beta a day later.

According to Databricks, a Workday admin sets up the connector by registering an Integration System User (ISU), the kind of system account Workday customers use for traditional integrations, with read access to the shared tables. After that, Unity Catalog permissions at the catalog, schema, and table level decide who can query the data.

Monroy said data lakes still make sense for analytics and for joining Workday data with the rest of a company’s data, but that an external lake is “the wrong place to build agents” that need governed access to Workday.

“You can export your data, but you can’t export the rules that govern the data,” he said, adding that rebuilding those rules in the lake means “maintaining a second copy” of Workday’s security model, “and the day it drifts, it’s all wrong.”

Everybody is losing their heads

Headless is the way to go right now, it seems. Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Microsoft, for example, already let outside agents into their systems of record. Salesforce launched Headless 360 at its TDX developer conference in April, so agents in Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, or a terminal can work with Salesforce data. ServiceNow made its Action Fabric MCP server generally available in May, with Anthropic as a launch partner, and Microsoft offers an MCP server for Dynamics 365 ERP.

All four vendors say outside agents stay within their existing permission models.

Whose identity does the agent use?

When it comes to agent identity, different vendors are currently taking very different approaches.

Salesforce, for example, is preparing to have agents that connect over MCP or its APIs register with their own credentials and permissions instead of acting under a user’s identity, according to Salesforce Ben. MCP clients will eventually need to switch to OAuth credentials tied to those agent identities.

Workday’s documentation says its agents can already get up to two system accounts of their own, called Agent System Users (ASUs), one for acting on a user’s behalf and one for “ambient” work, each with its own OAuth 2.0 client. Workday creates the ambient account automatically when a customer turns on an ambient skill.

Unified.to, which sells a Workday MCP integration, says every Workday MCP path, “official or not,” starts with creating an ISU. Cequence’s setup guide for its Workday MCP integration asks customers to create one “with appropriate security groups.” An agent working through an ISU sees whatever those security groups allow, no matter who is prompting it.

The more telling signal may be Kazmaier’s caveat. If building directly on the MCP server only works for a small set of use cases, the version of headless Workday expects most customers to use is Claude talking to Sana talking to Workday’s own agents, with Workday’s runtime in the middle of every call.

The post Workday goes headless, opening its HR and finance data to outside AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
Workday’s MCP server, SQL access, and agent runtime are now GA, letting developers build HR and finance agents in Claude Code and Cursor under user permissions.

item.title: The X Subscription bundles Cursor with Grok and X Premium. But Claude now costs extra.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Elon Musk’s mission to unify his sprawling tech empire continues apace, with the news that X, Grok, and Cursor are

The post The X Subscription bundles Cursor with Grok and X Premium. But Claude now costs extra. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk’s mission to unify his sprawling tech empire continues apace, with the news that X, Grok, and Cursor are being bundled together as a single plan dubbed The X Subscription.

Taking to X late on Monday, SpaceXAI announced the new pricing structure. It has five tiers, from free up to $200 per month, with the cheapest paid option costing $8. Paid tiers share a single pool of Grok-model usage across eligible products, and existing Cursor subscribers can keep their current plans — for now, at least.

However, arguably the bigger news for developers is the change to how Cursor charges for AI models. While the new subscriptions offer more included coding usage with Grok, customers who prefer competing models from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI will face additional charges.

Musk’s businesses come together

To rewind a little, Musk’s efforts to consolidate his businesses have been several years in the making. He acquired Twitter for $44 billion in October 2022, rebranding the social network as X the following July. That same month, he founded xAI, an OpenAI rival that unveiled its Grok chatbot later that year before making it available directly through X. In March 2025, the corporate structure changed again when xAI formally acquired X.

The consolidation continued back in February, when SpaceX acquired xAI, bringing Grok and X into the rocket company’s portfolio. Meanwhile, SpaceX agreed to buy AI coding company Cursor in a deal reportedly valued at $60 billion, which closed in mid-August. That same month, SpaceX launched Grok Bot, an autonomous AI assistant that can carry out tasks across third-party apps.

Some of these products were already bundled. X Premium has long included Grok, for example, and Cursor plans have included Grok Bot since August. But the X Subscription is the first plan to cover Cursor, Grok, Grok Bot, and X Premium together, with a single shared usage pool.

As an aside, SpaceXAI is in the midst of changing its name to SpaceXSI after Musk confirmed in early October that he would be following President Trump’s directive to use “super intelligence” (SI) in place of artificial intelligence (AI) — a move that is already reflected in its social media branding.

What the X Subscription means for Cursor users

The five tiers differ in the amount of AI usage they include, as well as which features customers can access. The free option offers limited use of Grok and Cursor’s coding agents, while the $8 Plus plan increases those allowances and adds X benefits, including a verification checkmark, creator tools, and fewer advertisements.

The $30 Premium tier is where the offering expands more substantially, adding access to Grok Bot, more advanced X features, and four times the AI usage included with Plus. The $100 Super plan increases that allowance to 15 times the Plus allocation, while the $200 Ultra tier raises it to 50 times. SpaceXAI says Premium combines benefits that previously cost $90 per month when purchased separately through SuperGrok, Cursor Pro, and X Premium+.

It’s also worth noting here that previously, its $20 Pro plan included cloud agents and Origin, the company’s GitHub alternative launched in August. Under The X Subscription, both features require at least the $30 Premium tier, meaning developers switching from the old Pro plan would have to pay an additional $10 per month to retain access to them.

For developers more broadly, there’s a pretty important distinction in how these various allowances work. Subscriptions come with a weekly allocation for using Grok models, which customers can draw on across Cursor, the Grok apps, and X. Grok Bot also consumes that allowance on eligible plans. So someone using Grok heavily for other activities could find themselves with less included usage available for coding. SpaceXAI, though, claims the new plans provide at least twice as much coding usage with its own models as comparable older Cursor subscriptions.

Third-party models now cost extra on Cursor

The economics of all this change considerably for developers who prefer to use third-party models from the frontier labs.

Previously, Cursor’s $20-per-month Pro plan included $20 worth of usage on third-party models such as Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s GPT and Google’s Gemini, calculated at their respective API prices. Cursor also provided additional usage beyond that allowance. Its $60 Pro+ and $200 Ultra plans included $70 and $400 worth of API-priced model usage respectively, before accounting for any additional allowances.

“The economics of all this change considerably for developers who prefer to use third-party models from the frontier labs.”

Under The X Subscription, access to third-party models starts with the $30 Premium tier, but the subscription fee no longer covers any of their usage. Instead, developers are charged at the models’ standard API rates from their very first request, with payments handled through prepaid credits. This applies even to customers paying $100 or $200 per month for the higher tiers.

To put that into perspective, a developer who previously paid $20 for Cursor Pro and consumed $20 worth of Claude usage could have had their entire bill covered by their subscription. Under the new Premium plan, that same usage would bring their monthly spending to $50 — comprising the $30 subscription and $20 in additional model charges.

“If most of your usage is on third-party models, the new plans might cost you more, so check your usage before switching.”

In a post on X explaining the changes, Matt Palmer, who works in developer experience at SpaceXAI, acknowledges that existing Cursor subscriptions effectively subsidize the use of competing AI models, allowing customers to access them at rates below what the providers charge directly.

“If most of your usage is on third-party models, the new plans might cost you more, so check your usage before switching,” Palmer writes. “That’s one of the main reasons these plans are opt-in.”

There are changes for businesses, too. Team subscriptions now start at $30 per user per month, down from the previous $40 entry-level Cursor Teams plan, with higher tiers available at $100 and $200. The company claims that its revised team offering provides three times more coding usage than its predecessor, alongside administrative features such as single sign-on, centralized billing and usage analytics.

Existing Cursor subscribers can continue with their current plans and included third-party model allowances for now. However, the announcement sparked a flurry of questions on Cursor’s community forum, particularly from existing Pro, Pro+ and Ultra subscribers trying to understand how the new plans compare with their current subscriptions. Some questioned whether switching would leave them paying more for the same usage, while others wanted to know whether they could simply stick with their existing plans indefinitely.

Responding to these concerns on Tuesday, Colin Mueller, a technical support engineer who joined SpaceXAI from Cursor in August, indicates that existing customers could stay put for the time being, though a mandatory transition may eventually be on the cards.

“Users who don’t choose to migrate will, sometime in the future, be migrated with advance notice.”

“Nothing happens to your Pro plan automatically,” Mueller writes. “You can keep it at the same price with the same features for now. Users who don’t choose to migrate will, sometime in the future, be migrated with advance notice.”

That would suggest a move to the new subscriptions is inevitable. But in a separate response to another user discussing the existing Ultra plan, Mueller is more cautious about what the company may or may not do.

“On how long the current plan lasts: it isn’t going away today, and there’s no timeline for moving remaining customers,” Mueller adds. “If that changes, you’ll get advance notice first.”

However, some developers are questioning what the changes mean for Cursor’s longstanding appeal as a platform that lets users choose between different AI models. One self-described longtime Ultra subscriber, posting under the username coco_max, argues that the new pricing risks alienating the developers who helped establish Cursor’s reputation, particularly those who rely heavily on Claude and GPT.

“Cursor earned its place next to Codex and Claude Code not because of its own model, but because it was ‘one editor where you can use the best models,’” the user writes. “A lot of us have all three installed, and Cursor is the one that stays open all day, precisely because it isn’t locked to any single vendor. The new plans change that.”

“Cursor earned its place next to Codex and Claude Code not because of its own model, but because it was ‘one editor where you can use the best models.’”

A battle over AI models and subscriptions

SpaceXAI’s pricing shake-up comes as Cursor is already losing access to one of its most popular model providers. In August, OpenAI announced plans to withdraw direct access to its models through Cursor, with a proposed cutoff date of November 12, citing concerns about Elon Musk’s track record on compliance with its terms of service.

Anthropic, for its part, pledged to continue supporting Claude in Cursor, despite competing directly with Grok. The relationship is complicated further by Anthropic’s multibillion-dollar agreement to purchase computing capacity from SpaceX.

There’s also a certain irony in the new pricing structure. Just last week, Musk confirmed that Grok Bot would use whichever AI model was best suited to a particular task, explicitly naming Anthropic’s Claude among the options. Yet developers who want to use Claude directly through Cursor now face additional charges under the new subscriptions.

Meanwhile, OpenAI is pursuing its own subscription strategy. At its DevDay conference in September, the company expanded its Sign in with ChatGPT offering, allowing paying subscribers to use their existing AI allowances inside third-party developer tools such as Devin, Amp and Warp. The move essentially gives OpenAI another way to keep developers using its models across competing products, without requiring separate API payments for eligible usage.

Ultimately, the new X Subscription raises questions about Cursor’s future as a model-agnostic coding platform. SpaceX clearly wants to encourage greater adoption of Grok, and its new pricing provides a financial incentive to do so. But with developers accustomed to choosing between Claude, GPT and other models, it remains to be seen whether the new offering will persuade them to embrace Grok — or prompt some to look elsewhere.

The post The X Subscription bundles Cursor with Grok and X Premium. But Claude now costs extra. appeared first on The New Stack.
SpaceXAI’s new plans promise more Grok usage for less, but Cursor users who prefer rival models will pay API rates from the first request.

item.title: “A major overhaul”: OpenCode 2.0 puts its terminal, desktop, and web apps on one shared service
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
OpenCode 2.0 is getting a formal unpacking today, some three months after its public beta launch. The sizable architectural upgrade

The post “A major overhaul”: OpenCode 2.0 puts its terminal, desktop, and web apps on one shared service appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenCode 2.0 is getting a formal unpacking today, some three months after its public beta launch. The sizable architectural upgrade introduces a shared background service connecting its terminal, web and desktop interfaces, alongside a rebuilt API, a new embeddable SDK, and support for running subagents and shell commands in the background.

In a blog post published on Monday, Anomaly, the company behind the open-source coding agent, calls the release a “major overhaul,” adding that it drew on the experiences of “millions of daily users” to build a more adaptable system capable of supporting an expanding range of agent capabilities.

Anomaly has, in fact, been iterating on version 2.0 over the past few months, including publishing a detailed technical account of its revamped plugin architecture and hot-reloading capabilities in September. However, the drawn-out rollout has caused some confusion among developers, with questions about whether version 2.0 was officially stable yet, and complaints about missing release notes, even as updates kept shipping.

Monday’s announcement, alongside the official changelog’s switch to the 2.x series, effectively signals that version 2 is now OpenCode’s main release. In tandem, the company is also offering a broader explanation of the technical decisions behind the upgrade.

OpenCode’s story so far

By way of a brief recap, OpenCode’s origins lie in the world of serverless development. Anomaly founders Jay V and Frank Wang previously created Serverless Stack (SST), an open-source framework for building and deploying applications on Amazon Web Services (AWS). Dax Raad, another prominent figure in OpenCode’s development, was also part of the SST team.

Since its 2025 debut, OpenCode has gained a fervent following among developers looking for greater freedom over the AI models powering their coding tools. That became particularly pertinent in January when Anthropic began preventing third-party agents from using Claude Pro and Max subscription credentials, forcing affected developers to find alternative ways of accessing Claude or switch providers.

As Janakiram MSV reported for The New Stack in May, these restrictions coincided with a surge of interest in OpenCode, which allows developers to switch between competing AI models. Today, the OpenCode GitHub repository has accumulated north of 212,000 stars and almost 30,000 forks.

More broadly, there are signs of growing commercial interest in this category of coding agents. In July, Anaconda acquired Kilo, another such open-source coding agent that allows developers to choose their preferred AI provider. Interestingly, Kilo had already rebuilt its command-line interface and VS Code extension using OpenCode, demonstrating how the latter was finding a role inside other developer tools.

With version 2.0, Anomaly has laid out how it has reworked OpenCode’s underlying architecture to accommodate a wider range of use cases. Arguably, the most significant change concerns how the coding agent runs, and how its different interfaces connect to it.

One service, multiple interfaces

Anomaly says the plumbing for a client/server setup has been in OpenCode from the start, though few beyond power users went out of their way to use it.

With version 2.0, the server now starts automatically as a single background process on the developer’s machine, allowing OpenCode’s terminal, browser and desktop interfaces to communicate with the same underlying service.

This means developers can access and manage their coding sessions through different interfaces, while the service handles the underlying execution. Scripts built using OpenCode’s programmatic client can also automatically discover and connect to the local service, making it useful for scheduled tasks, while developers can additionally expose the service to other machines and pair it with external applications.

“Developers can now start a session in OpenCode’s terminal interface, continue working on it through the desktop or web app, and have their own scripts connect to the same underlying service”.

The long and short of this is that developers can now start a session in OpenCode’s terminal interface, continue working on it through the desktop or web app, and have their own scripts connect to the same underlying service.

These architectural changes are accompanied by a ground-up redesign of OpenCode’s API, which Anomaly concedes was built piecemeal while the industry was still figuring things out.

“The old API grew haphazardly as we and the world collectively learned what agents are and should be,” the company writes in its blog post. “It was bad.”

“The old API grew haphazardly as we and the world collectively learned what agents are and should be. It was bad.”

And so the new API gives the agent greater control over its own environment. For example, it can create a Git worktree for a new task, transfer an existing session into that worktree, or identify and interrupt another session that has become stuck. Developers can also access the API through a new @opencode/client package, which supports standard JavaScript and Effect.

Another addition is an embeddable SDK, distributed as @opencode/sdk, that allows developers to incorporate OpenCode directly into their own applications. It uses the same underlying code as OpenCode’s CLI, the company notes, enabling developers to create customized versions of the agent for servers or environments such as Cloudflare Durable Objects.

These implementations can communicate with existing OpenCode clients through its standard server protocol, although Anomaly says the SDK remains under development.

Code Mode and background execution

OpenCode 2.0 also changes how agents interact with external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

A feature dubbed Code Mode allows agents to write JavaScript that calls multiple tools and processes their results within a single execution. Built around a lightweight JavaScript interpreter in the @opencode/codemode package, it converts MCP servers and OpenAPI endpoints into functions that agents can invoke programmatically.

For example, an agent could retrieve bug reports from GitHub, extract the relevant information and create corresponding issues in Linear, without having to make a separate model round trip for each operation.

The implications are particularly significant for developers connecting agents to large numbers of external services, where tool definitions can consume substantial portions of a model’s available context. Anomaly is making Code Mode the default for all MCP servers in version 2.0, arguing that it makes extensive integrations more practical.

“This means you can add a thousand of them with minimal context bloat and your agent will discover and compose them to get things done,” the company writes.

Meanwhile, OpenCode is introducing background execution for both subagents and shell commands, allowing developers to continue interacting with the primary agent while other operations are underway.

A developer could, for instance, delegate a code review to a subagent running a different AI model while continuing to work on the main task. Similarly, lengthy shell operations, such as running tests or building an application, can execute asynchronously, with the primary agent receiving a notification when they finish.

Developers can also use a keyboard shortcut to move an existing foreground task into the background if it takes longer than expected.

Rounding out the release are changes to OpenCode’s plugin architecture. Anomaly says it has implemented more than 80 internal plugins, covering most of the functionality introduced in version 2.0, as part of an effort to improve the reliability and maintainability of its plugin API.

Terminal interface plugins have also been promoted from experimental to stable, while support for hot reloading means OpenCode can create and start using a new plugin during an active session, without requiring a restart.

There are, however, some compatibility implications for existing users. Plugins developed for OpenCode 1.0 won’t work with version 2.0, while integrations built around the previous server API will need updating.

Existing OpenCode 1.x users can upgrade to version 2.0 by running opencode upgrade --major from the command line or entering /update in the terminal interface. According to the October 11 release notes, updates are no longer installed automatically, meaning users must initiate the upgrade themselves.

The post “A major overhaul”: OpenCode 2.0 puts its terminal, desktop, and web apps on one shared service appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenCode 2.0 entered public beta in July. Now, Anomaly explains the architectural overhaul, including a rebuilt API, an embeddable SDK and Code Mode.

item.title: GPUs on Kubernetes are bring-your-own-everything, starting with the bill
item.dc:creator: Yasmin Rajabi
item.description:
If you run a Kubernetes platform, you’ve probably got at least one Grafana dashboard for resource visibility on your workloads.

The post GPUs on Kubernetes are bring-your-own-everything, starting with the bill appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
If you run a Kubernetes platform, you’ve probably got at least one Grafana dashboard for resource visibility on your workloads. It shows what a container asked for versus what it used, making it relatively easy to point at the deployment that requested four cores and is only using half of one. If you break it down by namespace you get a rough idea which team is consuming what, which is what teams have been doing for CPU and memory for years and it mostly works.

Then people started putting workloads on GPUs and a lot of what we assumed would carry over didn’t. Almost every piece of visibility you take for granted on CPU and memory, GPUs make you build yourself. Your own metrics, your own accuracy, your own rules for splitting the bill. Which is what stings the most, since the GPU is the most expensive line on the bill.

Bring your own metrics

With CPU and memory, the kernel already tracks usage per container for you, so getting a per-pod number is basically free. GPUs on the other hand, don’t give you that. The tool everybody starts with, NVIDIA’s DCGM exporter, reports at the physical device level by default. This is fine when one pod has a GPU to itself, but the second you start sharing a GPU across pods, with time-slicing or MPS, DCGM gives every pod sharing that GPU the same value. So if three pods are sharing one GPU, all three look like they’re using the whole thing, and when you add it up you get 300% of a GPU that doesn’t exist. With time-slicing or MPS, the driver exposes a single set of counters for the whole GPU, so DCGM has no per-pod data to attribute and cannot distinguish which workload consumed what.

The numbers still plot nicely on a graph, but teams build full dashboards and reports on values that are blatantly wrong but hard to notice.

Bring your own rightsizing math

On the CPU side we’re all used to millicores, overcommitting, bursting, a CPU limit that just throttles you, a memory limit that gets you OOM killed but GPUs throw most of that out. A GPU shows up as a whole-number resource, nvidia.com/gpu: 1. You ask for whole GPUs, your request and your limit have to match, and there’s no overcommitting at the scheduler. The fractional sharing you need for inference happens underneath the scheduler through time-slicing or MIG, and Kubernetes requests don’t fit in neatly.

So the basic rightsizing premise, comparing what a workload requested against what it’s using and reclaiming the difference, barely exists for GPUs when you start. You end up having to work out how much of a GPU’s capacity a workload got before you can even have the waste conversation.

Bring your own guardrails

The NVIDIA container runtime looks at an environment variable called NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, and the base CUDA container images ship with it set to all. In a normal setup the device plugin overrides that and injects only the GPUs a pod was actually allocated. But if nothing overrides it or the container runtime is configured to honor the env var from the container, a pod can end up seeing and grabbing every GPU on the box no matter what Kubernetes thinks it handed out. So what the scheduler recorded as allocated and what ran on the hardware can diverge significantly. If you want the real number, you have to look at what’s happening at the process level and line it up against what Kubernetes thinks it did.

Bring your own definition of utilization

When a CPU graph says 80%, you pretty much know what you’re looking at, but GPU utilization is squishier. The usual metric tells you a kernel was running on the GPU for some slice of the sample window. It won’t tell you how much of the actual compute or memory bandwidth you burned. You can watch GPUs sit at 100% utilization while the compute is barely doing anything. And a lot of the time the thing that runs out first is memory, because frameworks like vLLM grab most of the GPU at startup whether they need it or not. Work out early which signal means something for your workloads, whether that’s compute occupancy, memory footprint, bandwidth, or power. If you rely on that big headline number, you can reach the wrong conclusion.

Bring your own attribution

NVIDIA’s NVML library will tell you, per process on a GPU, how much memory it’s holding, and you can trace each process back to the pod and team that owns it. The numbers are dependable, with one asterisk: they won’t quite add up to the card’s total, because the driver reserves a slice of memory for itself that doesn’t belong to any workload.

Compute is where it falls apart and it’s worth understanding why. Picture a shared kitchen: memory is counter space, you can look and see what ingredients are sitting where. Compute is the stove and everyone’s taking turns in bursts of milliseconds. What NVIDIA gives you isn’t “how much stove time did each cook get.” It’s closer to a flag that gets checked many times a second asking “was this cook doing something right now?” If two people are both working, both flags read yes almost all the time, so you get two jobs that each look 90% busy, which is true and also tells you nothing about who got more done.

That measurement is usable in one setup, when the GPU is strictly taking turns between jobs one at a time, where polling something like DCGM’s accounting mode or nvidia-smi’s PID-level sampling can approximate each job’s share. It breaks in the setup where jobs genuinely run side by side, which is also the setup people pick when they want better utilization. If two teams share a GPU, nothing available today will tell you which one burned 70% and which one burned 30%.

So the practical decision is to bill on memory, where the data holds up, and treat compute as a signal, something to drive chargeback. The reality is, fairness through accuracy between teams actually matters when you want to move beyond showback and GPU memory is the most accurate way to attribute with existing tooling.

Bring your own sharing paradigm

Sharing a GPU turns out to mean a handful of different things and each one changes the math underneath. There’s time-slicing, which round-robins the GPU with no isolation and lets you oversubscribe it. Then MPS lets kernels from different processes run at the same time. MIG is quite popular and splits the GPU into fixed hardware partitions, though it’s worth noting that most clouds still charge you for the whole physical GPU even when you’re only using a slice, and on A100/H100-class GPUs you can only slice it up to 7 instances. And then there’s DRA, Dynamic Resource Allocation, which has been maturing over the last few Kubernetes releases and is clearly where things are going, but the ecosystem around it, including autoscalers like Karpenter, is still catching up. Every one of these changes what “allocated” even means, so visibility depends on which mode a given node is in.

Bring your own splitting rules (and the bill is brutal)

GPU costs run far higher per hour than CPU costs and are much harder to split per workload. The cloud provider bills a GPU node as one line item with the CPU, memory, and GPU all lumped together. To get to a real dollar number per workload, you have to break that line apart and weight the GPU piece by model, because a T4 and an H200 are nowhere near the same price. Then you split it across whatever workloads were sharing the GPU. On AWS, the cheapest MIG compatible A100 GPU is $22/hr, about ~$14/hr on spot, whereas a comparable CPU-only instance of that size runs about $5/hr. Even on spot that’s quite the difference.

So what does this actually cost you?

Add this all up and the real cost isn’t just the GPU bill but the engineering time and toil you sink rebuilding visibility you used to get for free. The metrics, the expected accuracy, the guardrails, the attribution, the splitting rules, every layer is something you now have to own and maintain.

The upside here, is the space is moving quickly. DRA is maturing and adoption growing with it, hardware partitioning is getting easier, and the tooling gap narrows every release. So be deliberate about which layers you build now versus what you let the ecosystem catch up on, and definitely don’t go in expecting your CPU and memory playbook will carry straight over.

The post GPUs on Kubernetes are bring-your-own-everything, starting with the bill appeared first on The New Stack.

CPU and memory come with per-pod metrics, rightsizing and cost splits built in. Shared GPUs come with none of it, so platform teams end up rebuilding visibility for the most expensive line on the bill.

item.title: Google paid $90,000 for this bug, then waited two months to fix it
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google took two months to patch an unauthenticated RCE vulnerability in its developer documentation infrastructure. The problem was a reused

The post Google paid $90,000 for this bug, then waited two months to fix it appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google took two months to patch an unauthenticated RCE vulnerability in its developer documentation infrastructure. The problem was a reused OAuth client secret, which DevSite stored in a Flask session cookie and also used to sign sessions. Anyone who recovered the secret could forge a valid cookie and execute Python code on the server.

Simon Köck, a software engineer at Otark GmbH, discovered the flaw in Google’s DevSite infrastructure, the shared platform behind developers.google.com and several sibling documentation sites. Köck tells The New Stack that forged sessions were accepted on all seven affected domains, which relied on two different signing keys, and that he ran his code-execution proof on three of them, developers.google.com, docs.partner.android.com and web.dev.

Köck tells The New Stack that forged sessions were accepted on all seven affected domains, which relied on two different signing keys, and that he ran his code-execution proof on three of them

Google rated the vulnerability S0, the top of its severity scale, and awarded Köck a $90,000 bounty. That figure reflects a $75,000 base payout for an S0 RCE in what Google classifies as a normal application tier, multiplied by 1.2 for exceptional report quality.

Köck confirmed unauthenticated RCE with a Python sleep payload, measuring response delays that matched his payload, and deliberately stopped short of running commands or touching files, credentials, or internal services. “I’d call it an exceptionally serious RCE because anyone could reach it without an account or victim interaction,” he tells The New Stack, adding that he doesn’t know whether the three hosts he tested shared the same backend machines.

“I’d call it an exceptionally serious RCE because anyone could reach it without an account or victim interaction,”

The more consequential unknown sits behind the server itself. Köck tells The New Stack, Arvin Shivram, a Singapore-based researcher who goes by @brutecat and has reported more than 130 Google vulnerabilities by his own count, has since pointed out that internal App Engine apps often have access to Stubby, Google’s internal service-to-service communication system. Köck acknowledges that access “could be a major part of the impact,” though he says he didn’t verify what this particular DevSite process could reach.

One concern is whether an attacker could have modified Google’s developer documentation, replacing installation commands or download links with malicious ones. That could have enabled a supply-chain attack, but Köck didn’t test for write access to the content systems, and Google hasn’t disclosed DevSite’s process permissions or backend access.

The exposed key also let Köck forge DevSite sessions, though he stopped short of checking whether those sessions could impersonate users or reach anyone’s data. By his own accounting, the demonstrated impact amounts to code execution on three hosts and accepted forged sessions on seven, while the full blast radius, including any path into Google’s internal services, remains unproven.

One OAuth secret, two jobs

DevSite stored a serialized OAuth2WebServerFlow object from Google’s oauth2client library, which Google has deprecated in favor of google-auth, inside a Flask session cookie, exposing the OAuth client secret in the process. Google had also reused that same OAuth client secret as DevSite’s Flask session-signing key, which Köck confirmed by reproducing the cookie’s signature offline, giving him the ability to forge sessions the server would accept.

Pickle turns forgery into RCE

The OAuth callback used Python’s pickle to deserialize session data, so Köck swapped the flow object for a malicious pickle payload, signed the forged cookie and let the callback execute it. The chain depended on three mistakes lining up, a secret exposed in the cookie, that same secret doing double duty as a signing key, and unsafe deserialization of session data, and fixing any one of them would have broken it.

The chain depended on three mistakes lining up, a secret exposed in the cookie, that same secret doing double duty as a signing key, and unsafe deserialization of session data, and fixing any one of them would have broken it.

Patch pace raises questions

Köck reported the vulnerability on August 6, and Google accepted it the following day. The company approved the bounty on August 27 but didn’t deploy a fix until October 7.

Google hasn’t explained the two-month remediation window or whether it implemented interim mitigations, and questions also remain about the fix itself. Köck’s account of two separate signing keys explains why his recommendations mention two exposed OAuth client secrets, but Google hasn’t confirmed whether both were rotated or whether existing sessions were invalidated.

Köck tells The New Stack, he was never given a forensic conclusion and doesn’t know whether Google found evidence of exploitation before the patch, and the company hasn’t said either. Google had not responded to a request for comment as of this update.

An earlier version of this story said a single signing secret worked across all seven affected domains. Köck says the domains used two different signing keys. This story has also been updated with comment from Köck.
